name: Flipper Zero
firmware_note: The firmware it ships with. Region-locked sub-GHz TX, no BLE spam, no EMV, no Type 4 NFC emulation - conservative on purpose.
price_note: Direct from the vendor, in stock at time of checking. A microSD card is required and is not in the box. Grey-market resellers in countries where import is awkward charge well above this.
skill_note: The menus are genuinely approachable and you can do something useful on day one; understanding WHY an attack works is the hard part, not driving the device.
build_note: Works out of the box. Add a microSD card, run the mobile/desktop updater once, done.
summary: A pocket multitool built around four independent radios - a CC1101 sub-GHz transceiver, an ST25R3916 13.56 MHz NFC front end, a separate 125 kHz coil driven straight off the STM32, and the STM32WB55's own Bluetooth LE core - plus infrared, iButton and an 18-pin GPIO header. Stock firmware is the sane default: everything is signed, supported and gets security fixes, and the sub-GHz transmitter is restricted to what is legal where you provisioned the device. Best first stop for anyone learning RF and access control.
honest_take: The single biggest misconception is that it does Wi-Fi. It does not - there is no Wi-Fi radio in the device at all, and every Wi-Fi feature you have seen in a video is an ESP32 add-on board doing the work. The second is that stock firmware is crippled; it is not, it just will not transmit outside your region and will not ship the joke apps. For pure NFC research a Proxmark3 is far more capable, and for anything spectrum-shaped an RTL-SDR at a quarter the price sees vastly more.
best_for: Learning RF and access-control basics with good guardrails
Physical red-team work on legacy 125 kHz badge systems
Universal IR remote and everyday gate/garage cloning you are authorised to do
A first hardware-hacking device that will not brick itself
not_for: Wi-Fi attacks of any kind without the add-on board
Cracking modern rolling-code car keys
Serious NFC/smartcard research - get a Proxmark3
Spectrum analysis or anything needing IQ samples

hardware.mcu_primary_note: Dual core: Cortex-M4 @64MHz runs the application, Cortex-M0+ @32MHz runs the BLE stack. Linker script in the firmware confirms 1024K flash; 256KB SRAM total.

radios.note: TI CC1101 transceiver. Silicon is specified by TI for 300-348, 387-464 and 779-928 MHz only - it is NOT continuous 300-928 MHz. Max +12 dBm, OOK/ASK/2-FSK/4-FSK/GFSK/MSK, 0.6-600 kbps. Fixed-function transceiver, not an SDR.
13.56 MHz ONLY. Reader for ISO14443-3A/3B/4A/4B, ISO15693, FeliCa. It has nothing to do with the 125 kHz LF path.

125 kHz has NO dedicated chip. It is a discrete analog front end on its own separate coil, driven by the STM32: TIM1/TIM2 generate the carrier, COMP1 with a 1.2V internal reference demodulates the return. Confirmed in targets/f7/furi_hal/furi_hal_rfid.c.
Bluetooth LE only, on the M0+ coprocessor. There is NO Bluetooth Classic and no Wi-Fi anywhere in this device.
38 kHz IR receiver plus 3 discrete transmit LEDs. Learns and replays consumer IR.

hardware.battery_note: Li-Po. The firmware's fuel-gauge config (targets/f7/furi_hal/furi_hal_power_config.c) programs design capacity 2100 mAh; some spec sheets quote the cell as 2000 mAh nominal. Roughly a week idle, about a day of heavy RF use.
hardware.pmic: TI BQ25896 charger + TI BQ27220 fuel gauge
hardware.storage: microSD up to 256GB. NOT included, and the device is close to useless without one - all saved signals, cards, IR libraries and apps live on it.
hardware.gpio: 18-pin header, 3.3V logic (5V tolerant it is NOT). Exposes UART, SPI, I2C, 1-Wire and SWD. Pin 9 is a switchable 3.3V rail and pin 1 a switchable 5V rail, 1.2A max each, 5W total across the header; each I/O pin sources up to 20mA through a 51 ohm series resistor with ESD protection.
notable_physical: 5-way D-pad plus back button
IR window (TSOP-75338 receiver + 3 TX LEDs)
iButton / 1-Wire contact pad on the top edge
18-pin GPIO header
Two separate RFID antennas: a 125 kHz LF coil and a 13.56 MHz HF antenna
No external antenna connector of any kind

subghz_rx.note: 300-348 / 387-464 / 779-928 MHz via CC1101. RX is not region-restricted on any firmware.

subghz_replay.note: Capture and replay works reliably against STATIC-code devices: most older garage doors, gate remotes, barriers, some doorbells and cheap wireless sensors.

subghz_external_antenna.note: There is no SMA or u.FL connector. The antenna is internal and fixed.

subghz_amplified.note: CC1101 tops out around +12 dBm and there is no PA. Real-world range is tens of metres, not the hundreds people claim.

lf_125khz_read.note: EM4100/EM4102, HID Prox, Indala, IoProx and friends. Reads the ID off the card.

lf_125khz_write.note: Writes only to writable blank fobs (T5577, EM4305). You cannot rewrite a factory EM4100 or a real HID card - those are read-only silicon.

lf_125khz_emulate.note: Emulates saved LF credentials well. This is genuinely one of the things it is best at.

hf_1356_read.note: ISO14443-3A/3B/4A/4B, ISO15693, FeliCa, MIFARE Ultralight/Classic/Plus/DESFire, SLIX, ST25TB. 'Read' means UID plus whatever the card hands over without keys.

hf_1356_write.note: Only to 'magic'/gen1a-gen4 cards with a writable UID, which you have to buy separately. You cannot write a UID onto a normal card.

iso15693.note: Read and emulate ISO15693-3, plus SLIX variants.

felica.note: Reads FeliCa and has a listener, but no key material means Suica-style stored-value cards are read-only curiosities.

mifare_desfire.note: READ ONLY on every firmware. nfc_listener_defs.c has NULL for MfDesfire on official AND on all the community forks - DESFire emulation does not exist. Reading gets you the card's application/file structure and UID, not encrypted file contents, because AES/3DES keys are not recoverable.

ir_tx.note: 3 IR LEDs. Universal remote plus a large community IR database on the SD card.

ir_learn.note: Learns raw and decoded consumer IR protocols.

ir_universal_remote.note: Built in, with community-maintained code sets for TVs, ACs, projectors and audio gear.

ble_advertise.note: The STM32WB55's BLE core can advertise arbitrary payloads, which is what all the 'spam' and tag-emulation apps exploit.

ble_hid.note: Acts as a BLE keyboard/mouse - remote control apps and BLE-based BadUSB.

bt_classic.note: STM32WB55 is Bluetooth LE only. No A2DP, no Classic pairing, no BR/EDR sniffing. A common misconception.

ble_sniff.note: The BLE stack is a connectable peripheral/central stack, not a promiscuous sniffer. It cannot follow connections like an Ubertooth or a Sniffle dongle.

usb_hid_inject.note: BadUSB with Rubber Ducky-compatible scripts. Full-speed USB HID, enumerates as a keyboard.

usb_payload_lang.note: Ducky Script. Large community payload libraries.

uart.note: USB-to-UART bridge and an on-device UART terminal via the GPIO header.

i2c.note: I2C on the GPIO header; community i2ctools app.

jtag_swd.note: SWD only, not JTAG, and via community apps (SWD probe) or the Wi-Fi devboard running Black Magic Probe. Not a first-class debugger.

glitching.note: No fault-injection hardware - no crowbar, no precise clock/voltage glitch path.

ibutton_1wire.note: Reads, writes and emulates Dallas/Cyfral/Metakom iButton keys. Niche outside eastern Europe but works properly.

gps.note: Needs a UART GPS module on the GPIO header.

sd_logging.note: Everything is stored on the microSD card as readable files.

scriptable.note: JavaScript engine (js_app) is built into official firmware and every fork; plus C apps via the SDK.

standalone_untethered.note: Fully self-contained on battery - no phone or laptop required for its core functions.

wifi_scan_24.note: Requires the official Flipper Zero Wi-Fi Dev Board (ESP32-S2) or a third-party ESP32 on the GPIO header. The Flipper itself has no Wi-Fi radio.

wifi_scan_5.note: No firmware or add-on board in this ecosystem does 5 GHz. The official devboard's ESP32-S2 is 2.4 GHz only.

wifi_monitor_mode.note: On the ESP32 add-on, not on the Flipper. Promiscuous mode on ESP32, not true monitor mode with full radiotap.

wifi_deauth_24.note: Runs entirely on an ESP32 add-on flashed with ESP32 Marauder or similar. The Flipper is only a screen, keypad and battery for it.

wifi_evil_twin.note: Evil Portal / Marauder on the ESP32 add-on board.

wifi_captive_portal.note: Evil Portal app drives an ESP32 add-on; the portal HTML lives on the Flipper's SD card.

wifi_handshake_capture.note: ESP32 Marauder on the add-on board. Capture quality is well below a proper Wi-Fi adapter in monitor mode.

wifi_pmkid.note: ESP32 Marauder on the add-on board.

wifi_beacon_spam.note: ESP32 Marauder on the add-on board.

wifi_probe_sniff.note: ESP32 Marauder on the add-on board.

wifi_wardriving.note: Wardriver / Marauder companion apps log WiGLE-format CSV, but need both an ESP32 board and a GPS module on the GPIO header.

nrf24_scan.note: Needs an nRF24L01+ module wired to the GPIO header. Apps exist in the community app packs.

mousejack.note: MouseJacker app plus an nRF24L01+ module on GPIO. Only works against unpatched 2.4 GHz keyboard/mouse dongles, a shrinking target set.

sdr_rx.note: Not an SDR. The CC1101 is a fixed-function narrowband transceiver - you tune it to a frequency and modulation, you do not get IQ samples.

subghz_tx.note: REGION-LOCKED. The firmware has a 'region' service; the provisioning app sets your region on first update and TX is limited to that region's civil allow-list - e.g. EU gets 433.05-434.79 and 868.15-868.55 MHz, US/Americas get 304.10-321.95 and 915-928 MHz. Try anything else and it refuses with 'transmission on this frequency is restricted in your region'. RX stays unrestricted.

subghz_rolling_code.note: It can RECORD a rolling-code transmission and tell you the protocol (KeeLoq, Security+ 2.0, Somfy, etc.), but replaying a captured code does not work by design - the receiver has already moved past it. Stock firmware deliberately ships no rolling-code bypass.

subghz_bruteforce.note: No brute-force app in stock firmware. Community apps add it, and it only ever helps against short static codes such as 8-12 bit DIP-switch remotes.

mifare_classic_attacks.note: Dictionary attack against known/default keys runs on device. The mfkey32 READER attack also runs on device (via the mfkey app from the catalog): you emulate the card at a real reader, collect nonces, and crack Crypto-1 - minutes on the Flipper's CPU. What you cannot do on stock is a card-only attack - no nested/hardnested is built in.

nfc_type4_ndef.note: Official firmware has an ISO14443-4A listener and an NDEF parser plugin, so it reads NDEF fine. It has NO Type4Tag or Ntag4xx protocol module - those exist only in the community forks - so it cannot present itself as a writable NDEF Type 4 tag.

emv_read.note: Official firmware has only a small helper table (nfc_emv_parser.c) that resolves EMV application IDs and currency codes for other parsers. There is NO EMV poller in the official tree - the protocol module does not exist. You cannot 'read a bank card' on stock firmware.

hf_1356_emulate.note: Emulation exists for ISO14443-3A, ISO14443-4A, ISO15693-3, MIFARE Ultralight, MIFARE Classic, SLIX and FeliCa. It does NOT exist for ISO14443-3B, ISO14443-4B, DESFire or ST25TB - those entries are NULL in nfc_listener_defs.c.

ble_scan.note: No BLE scanner app in stock firmware.

ble_spam_apple.note: Not in official firmware. Community forks only.

findmy_track.note: The FindMy Flipper app is not part of official firmware.

magspoof.note: Needs external magspoof coil hardware on GPIO plus a community app; not a stock feature.

usb_mass_storage.note: Available as a catalog app rather than built in.

spi_flash_dump.note: Via the community SPI Mem Manager app and test clips; not built in.

logic_analyzer.note: Community app only, low sample rate - fine for slow buses, not a replacement for a real analyser.

import_restricted: Delaware, USA - THE STRICTEST PROVISION FOUND ANYWHERE, and it is IN FORCE. 21 Del. C. section 6711 (added by 85 Del. Laws c.393, signed 2026-07-23) makes it an offence to knowingly possess, manufacture, sell, transfer or offer a 'vehicle security circumvention device', defined to include 'any other device ... designed or used to intercept the signal from the key fob of a motor vehicle'. Note what is and is not required: you must KNOWINGLY possess the device, but there is NO requirement that you intended to use it to steal a car. The exemption list is closed and covers law enforcement, the National Insurance Crime Bureau, dealers, distributors, manufacturers, mechanics, locksmiths and repossession agents - security researchers and hobbyists are NOT on it. Whether a general-purpose device like a Flipper Zero falls inside that definition is arguable and appears untested, but anyone in Delaware should take advice rather than assume it does not.

United Kingdom - ENACTED BUT NOT YET IN FORCE. Crime and Policing Act 2026 (c.20) section 149, Royal Assent 2026-04-29, creates an offence of possessing, importing, making, adapting or supplying an electronic device 'in circumstances which give rise to a reasonable suspicion that the device will be used in connection with' vehicle theft, with up to 5 years on indictment and a defence the defendant must prove. legislation.gov.uk marks section 149 'Prospective' and none of the commencement orders made so far brings it into force. Some outlets are already reporting it as live law; it is not. Until it is commenced, the Flipper is legal to own and is sold direct into the UK under a UKCA Declaration of Conformity.

Brazil - the only genuine national restriction anywhere, and it is narrower than reported. ANATEL closed the simplified self-declaration homologation route for this product in March 2023, treating it like signal jammers and illicit TV boxes, under Resolution 715/2019 art. 60, II (homologation must be refused where a product serves illicit ends). Certification is compulsory under LGT art. 162 para 2, so uncertified units get held at customs. Three things are commonly got wrong: POSSESSION is not an offence (LGT art. 162 para 2 prohibits use, and Res. 715/2019 art. 83's list of sanctionable conduct omits possession; penalties are administrative); it is NOT established that the manufacturer applied and was refused, as the outlet that reported it published an errata saying users rather than Flipper Devices approached ANATEL; and the much-quoted '340+ seizures' figure is from March 2023 and has never been updated, so it must not be presented as current. Res. 715/2019 art. 88 provides a research/experimental import waiver on paper, but no granted case is documented. Marketplace delistings (Mercado Livre, OLX) were their own terms of service, though Res. 780/2025 has since made marketplaces jointly liable for non-homologated listings.

Canada - the popular story is wrong in BOTH directions. The February 2024 'ban' was indeed withdrawn: ISED announced it on 2024-02-08 and by 2024-03-20 had revised it to restricting use by illegitimate actors. The device is ISED-certified (Technical Acceptance Certificate 27624-FZ) and the vendor lists Canada as 'Direct sale' today. BUT it is not true that nothing was enacted - Bill C-69 (2024, c.17, ss.380-382) amended the Radiocommunication Act to add s.4(5) and s.5.01, in force since 2024-06-20, giving the minister power to specify by order devices whose possession, import and sale are then prohibited, with penalties to $25,000 for individuals and $10,000,000 for corporations. No order has ever been made under s.5.01 and the Flipper Zero has never been specified; the follow-up consultation (Gazette Notice DGSO-003-24, closed August 2024) named seven categories of purpose-built auto-theft tool and did NOT name the Flipper Zero, and produced no decision document. Public Safety's own status page as of May 2025 still records ISED as 'evaluating potential approaches'. The accurate line is 'the power to ban it exists and has sat unused for over two years', not 'nothing happened'.

United States (federal) - NOT restricted. The device holds three FCC Grants of Equipment Authorization under FCC ID 2A2V6-FZ, all dated 2022-01-14, covering 2.4 GHz DTS, Part 15 security/remote control on 304.5-321.95 / 433.075-434.775 / 915-927.95 MHz, and 13.56 MHz. The FCC has never issued an advisory or enforcement action naming it. CBP held a container of about 15,000 units from September to October 2022 and released them roughly a month later with no reason given, and there have been no seizures since. Amazon delisted it on 2023-04-07 as a 'card skimming device' and eBay listings have been blocked since around October 2022, but marketplace policies are not law. It is legal to own and buy federally - but see Delaware above, and expect more states to legislate.

California, USA - IN FORCE but a poor fit. Penal Code s.466, as amended by AB 486 (Ch. 367 of 2025) effective 2026-01-01, adds 'key programming device', 'key duplicating device' and 'signal extender' to the burglary-tools list. Unlike Delaware it REQUIRES intent to feloniously break or enter, and the definitions target devices that access a vehicle's onboard computer or amplify a fob's range - arguably not what a Flipper Zero does. Listed for completeness rather than as a live risk.

European Union - NOT restricted, and legally placed on the market in all 27 member states. Flipper Devices holds an EU Declaration of Conformity under the Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU plus RoHS for model FZ.1, self-declared, which is lawful under RED Annex II where harmonised standards are applied. There are no EU Safety Gate/RAPEX alerts for the device or the company, and it appears on no market-restriction register in Germany, the Netherlands, Poland, France or Italy. Sold direct into the EU.

Australia - NOT restricted. No ACMA prohibition, no Australian Border Force import prohibition (its 74-item list has no RF multi-tool category), and no state device ban. The device has a registered Australian RCM Supplier's Declaration of Conformity for model FZ.1 dated 2022 - note that is a 2022 declaration citing notices since superseded, so read it as 'has a registered RCM declaration', not 'is currently certified'. Sold locally through resellers. State provisions such as NSW Crimes Act ss.308F/308G/192L and QLD Criminal Code s.408E are intent-gated conduct offences, not device bans. Ignore the widely-syndicated claim that Australia enacted 'unauthorised signal-capture device' rules on 2026-07-01 with AU$55,000 penalties - no such scheme exists and the claim appears to be fabricated.
legal.notes: Owning a Flipper Zero is legal in the US, the UK, the EU and most of the world - the device is CE/FCC marked and sold openly by the vendor. What gets people in trouble is USE, not ownership: transmitting on sub-GHz frequencies you are not licensed for, opening a gate or car that is not yours, cloning an access credential without permission, or interfering with a radio service are separate offences almost everywhere, and they are the offences people actually get charged with. Note also that the community firmwares remove a region lock that exists specifically to keep you inside your national band plan - once you flash one, staying legal is on you. Be careful with the reporting on this device: several widely-repeated 'bans' were proposals that were dropped, marketplace policies, or one-off customs and airport-security incidents rather than law - and at least one site publishes an entirely fabricated Australian restriction that has no basis at all. The real trend to watch is different and newer: legislators have moved away from naming the Flipper and towards banning possession of 'vehicle security circumvention' or 'key fob signal' devices as a CLASS, sometimes without requiring any intent to steal and without exempting researchers. Delaware has such a law in force; the UK has one passed but not yet commenced; Canada has given itself the power to make one. If you own one of these devices, that class-based drafting is what should be on your radar, not the 2024 headlines. Alongside those, most countries already have INTENT-BASED offences that catch misuse without touching ownership: Canada's Criminal Code s.333.2 (in force 2024-07-20, possessing a device suitable for vehicle theft FOR THE PURPOSE of committing it, max 10 years - Justice Canada's own note says that absent intent, possession is not an offence), and in the US 18 U.S.C. 1029 access-device fraud, 18 U.S.C. 1030 (CFAA), 47 U.S.C. 301/302a/333 for unlicensed transmission and interference, and the Wiretap Act. Finally, be sceptical of specific claims: no country has ever enacted a law banning the Flipper Zero BY NAME, and reported bans in Thailand and India trace to unsourced or AI-generated pages with no regulator announcement behind them. Treat this as 'check your own local law', not legal advice.

Legal position was checked against primary sources for the US (federal and Delaware), UK, EU, Canada, Brazil and Australia, and the two highest-impact claims - Delaware 21 Del. C. s.6711 and UK Crime and Policing Act 2026 s.149 - were read directly on delcode.delaware.gov and legislation.gov.uk rather than taken from reporting. Remaining soft spots: no dated primary ANATEL document was located for the Brazilian position (it rests on ANATEL's published reasoning plus a TeleSintese errata); whether a general-purpose device such as the Flipper Zero actually falls within Delaware's 'vehicle security circumvention device' definition appears untested in court; US states other than Delaware were not systematically surveyed and more are likely to legislate; and the vendor's per-country sales table is weak evidence about legality, since 235 of its 301 listed territories have no sales channel for ordinary commercial reasons. Also unconfirmed: Delaware s.6711's penalty grade is not stated in the codified section, so none is published here; no ANATEL act or process number naming the device could be retrieved (ANATEL's registers sit behind SSO and its news URLs block automated fetches); no granted Brazilian research-import authorisation is documented; eBay's delisting has no official public statement; and no systematic 50-state US survey was possible, so more states may have comparable laws - Michigan in particular has had key-programmer bills since 2024 with no confirmed enactment, and nothing should be published about it.

firmware_note: The polished fork: unlocked sub-GHz TX, deep UI/theming customisation, and BLE Spam, FindMy and NFC Maker compiled in. Direct continuation of Xtreme by the same developers.

honest_take: It is a very well-built fork, but almost everything people credit it with is either an APP that also runs on other firmware, or a hardware capability that was always there and was only being withheld by policy. Also note the release cadence - the last tagged stable is mntm-012 from 2025-12-31 and everything since has been dev builds.

subghz_rx.note: 300-348 / 387-464 / 779-928 MHz via CC1101. RX is not region-restricted on any firmware.

subghz_replay.note: Capture and replay works reliably against STATIC-code devices: most older garage doors, gate remotes, barriers, some doorbells and cheap wireless sensors.

subghz_external_antenna.note: The Flipper still has no antenna connector, but community firmware supports an EXTERNAL CC1101 module over GPIO (hardware SPI), and those modules do have SMA connectors and sometimes an amplifier.

subghz_amplified.note: Only via an external amplified CC1101 module on the GPIO header; the internal radio is unchanged.

lf_125khz_read.note: EM4100/EM4102, HID Prox, Indala, IoProx and friends. Reads the ID off the card.

lf_125khz_write.note: Writes only to writable blank fobs (T5577, EM4305). You cannot rewrite a factory EM4100 or a real HID card - those are read-only silicon.

lf_125khz_emulate.note: Emulates saved LF credentials well. This is genuinely one of the things it is best at.

hf_1356_read.note: ISO14443-3A/3B/4A/4B, ISO15693, FeliCa, MIFARE Ultralight/Classic/Plus/DESFire, SLIX, ST25TB. 'Read' means UID plus whatever the card hands over without keys.

hf_1356_write.note: Only to 'magic'/gen1a-gen4 cards with a writable UID, which you have to buy separately. You cannot write a UID onto a normal card.

iso15693.note: Read and emulate ISO15693-3, plus SLIX variants.

felica.note: Reads FeliCa and has a listener, but no key material means Suica-style stored-value cards are read-only curiosities.

mifare_desfire.note: READ ONLY on every firmware. nfc_listener_defs.c has NULL for MfDesfire on official AND on all the community forks - DESFire emulation does not exist. Reading gets you the card's application/file structure and UID, not encrypted file contents, because AES/3DES keys are not recoverable.

ir_tx.note: 3 IR LEDs. Universal remote plus a large community IR database on the SD card.

ir_learn.note: Learns raw and decoded consumer IR protocols.

ir_universal_remote.note: Built in, with community-maintained code sets for TVs, ACs, projectors and audio gear.

ble_advertise.note: The STM32WB55's BLE core can advertise arbitrary payloads, which is what all the 'spam' and tag-emulation apps exploit.

ble_hid.note: Acts as a BLE keyboard/mouse - remote control apps and BLE-based BadUSB.

bt_classic.note: STM32WB55 is Bluetooth LE only. No A2DP, no Classic pairing, no BR/EDR sniffing. A common misconception.

ble_sniff.note: The BLE stack is a connectable peripheral/central stack, not a promiscuous sniffer. It cannot follow connections like an Ubertooth or a Sniffle dongle.

usb_hid_inject.note: BadUSB with Rubber Ducky-compatible scripts. Full-speed USB HID, enumerates as a keyboard.

usb_payload_lang.note: Ducky Script. Large community payload libraries.

uart.note: USB-to-UART bridge and an on-device UART terminal via the GPIO header.

i2c.note: I2C on the GPIO header; community i2ctools app.

jtag_swd.note: SWD only, not JTAG, and via community apps (SWD probe) or the Wi-Fi devboard running Black Magic Probe. Not a first-class debugger.

glitching.note: No fault-injection hardware - no crowbar, no precise clock/voltage glitch path.

ibutton_1wire.note: Reads, writes and emulates Dallas/Cyfral/Metakom iButton keys. Niche outside eastern Europe but works properly.

gps.note: Needs a UART GPS module on the GPIO header.

sd_logging.note: Everything is stored on the microSD card as readable files.

scriptable.note: JavaScript engine (js_app) is built into official firmware and every fork; plus C apps via the SDK.

standalone_untethered.note: Fully self-contained on battery - no phone or laptop required for its core functions.

wifi_scan_24.note: Requires the official Flipper Zero Wi-Fi Dev Board (ESP32-S2) or a third-party ESP32 on the GPIO header. The Flipper itself has no Wi-Fi radio.

wifi_scan_5.note: No firmware or add-on board in this ecosystem does 5 GHz. The official devboard's ESP32-S2 is 2.4 GHz only.

wifi_monitor_mode.note: On the ESP32 add-on, not on the Flipper. Promiscuous mode on ESP32, not true monitor mode with full radiotap.

wifi_deauth_24.note: Runs entirely on an ESP32 add-on flashed with ESP32 Marauder or similar. The Flipper is only a screen, keypad and battery for it.

wifi_evil_twin.note: Evil Portal / Marauder on the ESP32 add-on board.

wifi_captive_portal.note: Evil Portal app drives an ESP32 add-on; the portal HTML lives on the Flipper's SD card.

wifi_handshake_capture.note: ESP32 Marauder on the add-on board. Capture quality is well below a proper Wi-Fi adapter in monitor mode.

wifi_pmkid.note: ESP32 Marauder on the add-on board.

wifi_beacon_spam.note: ESP32 Marauder on the add-on board.

wifi_probe_sniff.note: ESP32 Marauder on the add-on board.

wifi_wardriving.note: Wardriver / Marauder companion apps log WiGLE-format CSV, but need both an ESP32 board and a GPS module on the GPIO header.

nrf24_scan.note: Needs an nRF24L01+ module wired to the GPIO header. Apps exist in the community app packs.

mousejack.note: MouseJacker app plus an nRF24L01+ module on GPIO. Only works against unpatched 2.4 GHz keyboard/mouse dongles, a shrinking target set.

sdr_rx.note: Not an SDR. The CC1101 is a fixed-function narrowband transceiver - you tune it to a frequency and modulation, you do not get IQ samples.

subghz_tx.note: Region lock removed. Momentum additionally offers an EXTENDED range of 281-361 / 378-481 / 749-962 MHz, which is outside the CC1101's TI-specified bands - performance there is poor because the antenna match is wrong, and the projects warn it can damage the hardware. Legality is entirely on you.

subghz_rolling_code.note: Be precise here. Community firmware lets you SAVE and re-send captured rolling-code signals, and adds manual creation/pairing for protocols like KeeLoq, FAAC SLH, BFT Mitto, Somfy Telis, Nice Flor-S, CAME Atomo and Security+ 2.0 - that is programming a NEW remote into a receiver you control, which needs physical access to the receiver's learn button. It does NOT let you clone someone's rolling-code remote from a captured press. The genuine exception is the RollBack class of attack (Csikor et al., arXiv:2210.11923): replaying two or more consecutively captured codes can roll a receiver's counter back and make old codes valid again. That is implemented openly in the 'rolling_flaws' app and is what the 2025 'DarkWeb firmware' stories were repackaging. Even where it works it only reaches the LOCK/UNLOCK remote-keyless-entry function on some brands - it does NOT touch the immobiliser, so it does not start a car.

subghz_bruteforce.note: Sub-GHz Bruteforcer app included. Only meaningful against short STATIC codes - 8-12 bit DIP-switch style remotes and some fixed-code gates. It will not brute-force a rolling code in any useful timeframe.

mifare_classic_attacks.note: Best-in-class for a device this cheap, but know the boundary. On device: dictionary attack against known keys, and the mfkey32 READER attack (emulate the card at a real reader, harvest nonces, recover Crypto-1 keys in a few minutes). Community firmware also adds card-only nested attack collection. What still generally needs a PC is the heavy maths: hardnested and full nested recovery, where the Flipper collects nonces into a .nested.log and a desktop tool or web service does the cracking. Static nested can be finished on device. Once keys are known it emulates the card and can write to 'magic' cards.

nfc_type4_ndef.note: This is a genuine community-firmware-only capability. The forks add Type4Tag and Ntag4xx protocol modules that official firmware does not have: they READ NTAG 4xx and generic ISO14443-4 Type 4 tags, and there is a Type4Tag LISTENER, so the Flipper can present itself as an NDEF Type 4 tag (this is what the NFC Maker app uses to serve URLs, Wi-Fi credentials, contact cards). Note Ntag4xx itself is read-only - its listener entry is NULL - and DESFire emulation does not exist on any firmware.

emv_read.note: Community firmware has a real EMV poller, so it can read the openly-readable side of a contactless bank card: PAN, expiry, cardholder name where present, and sometimes a transaction log. That is NOT cloning - it cannot produce the dynamic cryptogram a terminal demands, so it cannot pay. Worth knowing: the EMV plugin was silently BROKEN for a long stretch - it shipped as a plugin that never loaded at all - and was only fixed in Unleashed PR #1073, merged 2026-08-20, then flowed downstream. If you used a build from before late August 2026, EMV appeared to be supported but did nothing.

hf_1356_emulate.note: Emulation exists for ISO14443-3A, ISO14443-4A, ISO15693-3, MIFARE Ultralight, MIFARE Classic, MIFARE Plus, SLIX, FeliCa and generic Type 4 Tag. Still NULL and therefore impossible: ISO14443-3B, ISO14443-4B, DESFire, ST25TB, NTAG4xx.

magspoof.note: MagSpoof app is bundled, but it needs an external coil/H-bridge on the GPIO header to actually emit a magstripe field.

usb_mass_storage.note: Mass Storage app bundled - the Flipper presents an SD-card image as a USB drive.

spi_flash_dump.note: SPI Mem Manager app is bundled; you still need test clips/wires to reach the chip.

logic_analyzer.note: Bundled community app. Low sample rate - fine for UART/I2C at modest speeds, not a bench analyser.

ble_scan.note: Community BLE scanner/tracker-detector apps exist in the app packs; not a core firmware feature.

ble_spam_apple.note: Apple Continuity (proximity-pair popups, Nearby Action modals). Real, but oversold. The STM32WB55 BLE stack advertises one payload at a time and cycles through them, so this is protocol-level nuisance advertising, not RF jamming and not a flood. Apple (iOS 17.2+), Google, Microsoft and Samsung all added cooldowns and sanity checks after 2023, so on current phones it is mostly a party trick. The app's own author describes it that way.

The STM32WB55 BLE stack advertises one payload at a time and cycles through them, so this is protocol-level nuisance advertising, not RF jamming and not a flood. Apple (iOS 17.2+), Google, Microsoft and Samsung all added cooldowns and sanity checks after 2023, so on current phones it is mostly a party trick. The app's own author describes it that way.

The STM32WB55 BLE stack advertises one payload at a time and cycles through them, so this is protocol-level nuisance advertising, not RF jamming and not a flood. Apple (iOS 17.2+), Google, Microsoft and Samsung all added cooldowns and sanity checks after 2023, so on current phones it is mostly a party trick. The app's own author describes it that way.

ble_spam_swift_pair.note: Microsoft Swift Pair - shows on Windows where Swift Pair notifications are enabled, which is the Windows 10/11 default. Real, but oversold. The STM32WB55 BLE stack advertises one payload at a time and cycles through them, so this is protocol-level nuisance advertising, not RF jamming and not a flood. Apple (iOS 17.2+), Google, Microsoft and Samsung all added cooldowns and sanity checks after 2023, so on current phones it is mostly a party trick. The app's own author describes it that way.

findmy_track.note: Read this carefully because the name misleads everyone: FindMy Flipper does NOT find or track other people's AirTags. It turns the Flipper itself INTO a trackable tag, broadcasting a BLE beacon that Apple's Find My network (or Samsung SmartThings / Tile) picks up, so YOU can locate your own Flipper. Setup is either cloning an existing tag's MAC and payload (which requires killing the original tag's battery so it stops rotating keys) or generating OpenHaystack key pairs with Docker/Python on a PC and importing a .keys file. It is an app, not a radio feature - the underlying hardware capability is just 'BLE can advertise'.

ble_tracker_detect.note: Separate community apps scan for tracker advertisements and match on service UUID / manufacturer data. Not the same thing as FindMy Flipper, and not a firmware feature.

import_restricted: Delaware, USA - THE STRICTEST PROVISION FOUND ANYWHERE, and it is IN FORCE. 21 Del. C. section 6711 (added by 85 Del. Laws c.393, signed 2026-07-23) makes it an offence to knowingly possess, manufacture, sell, transfer or offer a 'vehicle security circumvention device', defined to include 'any other device ... designed or used to intercept the signal from the key fob of a motor vehicle'. Note what is and is not required: you must KNOWINGLY possess the device, but there is NO requirement that you intended to use it to steal a car. The exemption list is closed and covers law enforcement, the National Insurance Crime Bureau, dealers, distributors, manufacturers, mechanics, locksmiths and repossession agents - security researchers and hobbyists are NOT on it. Whether a general-purpose device like a Flipper Zero falls inside that definition is arguable and appears untested, but anyone in Delaware should take advice rather than assume it does not.

United Kingdom - ENACTED BUT NOT YET IN FORCE. Crime and Policing Act 2026 (c.20) section 149, Royal Assent 2026-04-29, creates an offence of possessing, importing, making, adapting or supplying an electronic device 'in circumstances which give rise to a reasonable suspicion that the device will be used in connection with' vehicle theft, with up to 5 years on indictment and a defence the defendant must prove. legislation.gov.uk marks section 149 'Prospective' and none of the commencement orders made so far brings it into force. Some outlets are already reporting it as live law; it is not. Until it is commenced, the Flipper is legal to own and is sold direct into the UK under a UKCA Declaration of Conformity.

Brazil - the only genuine national restriction anywhere, and it is narrower than reported. ANATEL closed the simplified self-declaration homologation route for this product in March 2023, treating it like signal jammers and illicit TV boxes, under Resolution 715/2019 art. 60, II (homologation must be refused where a product serves illicit ends). Certification is compulsory under LGT art. 162 para 2, so uncertified units get held at customs. Three things are commonly got wrong: POSSESSION is not an offence (LGT art. 162 para 2 prohibits use, and Res. 715/2019 art. 83's list of sanctionable conduct omits possession; penalties are administrative); it is NOT established that the manufacturer applied and was refused, as the outlet that reported it published an errata saying users rather than Flipper Devices approached ANATEL; and the much-quoted '340+ seizures' figure is from March 2023 and has never been updated, so it must not be presented as current. Res. 715/2019 art. 88 provides a research/experimental import waiver on paper, but no granted case is documented. Marketplace delistings (Mercado Livre, OLX) were their own terms of service, though Res. 780/2025 has since made marketplaces jointly liable for non-homologated listings.

Canada - the popular story is wrong in BOTH directions. The February 2024 'ban' was indeed withdrawn: ISED announced it on 2024-02-08 and by 2024-03-20 had revised it to restricting use by illegitimate actors. The device is ISED-certified (Technical Acceptance Certificate 27624-FZ) and the vendor lists Canada as 'Direct sale' today. BUT it is not true that nothing was enacted - Bill C-69 (2024, c.17, ss.380-382) amended the Radiocommunication Act to add s.4(5) and s.5.01, in force since 2024-06-20, giving the minister power to specify by order devices whose possession, import and sale are then prohibited, with penalties to $25,000 for individuals and $10,000,000 for corporations. No order has ever been made under s.5.01 and the Flipper Zero has never been specified; the follow-up consultation (Gazette Notice DGSO-003-24, closed August 2024) named seven categories of purpose-built auto-theft tool and did NOT name the Flipper Zero, and produced no decision document. Public Safety's own status page as of May 2025 still records ISED as 'evaluating potential approaches'. The accurate line is 'the power to ban it exists and has sat unused for over two years', not 'nothing happened'.

United States (federal) - NOT restricted. The device holds three FCC Grants of Equipment Authorization under FCC ID 2A2V6-FZ, all dated 2022-01-14, covering 2.4 GHz DTS, Part 15 security/remote control on 304.5-321.95 / 433.075-434.775 / 915-927.95 MHz, and 13.56 MHz. The FCC has never issued an advisory or enforcement action naming it. CBP held a container of about 15,000 units from September to October 2022 and released them roughly a month later with no reason given, and there have been no seizures since. Amazon delisted it on 2023-04-07 as a 'card skimming device' and eBay listings have been blocked since around October 2022, but marketplace policies are not law. It is legal to own and buy federally - but see Delaware above, and expect more states to legislate.

California, USA - IN FORCE but a poor fit. Penal Code s.466, as amended by AB 486 (Ch. 367 of 2025) effective 2026-01-01, adds 'key programming device', 'key duplicating device' and 'signal extender' to the burglary-tools list. Unlike Delaware it REQUIRES intent to feloniously break or enter, and the definitions target devices that access a vehicle's onboard computer or amplify a fob's range - arguably not what a Flipper Zero does. Listed for completeness rather than as a live risk.

European Union - NOT restricted, and legally placed on the market in all 27 member states. Flipper Devices holds an EU Declaration of Conformity under the Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU plus RoHS for model FZ.1, self-declared, which is lawful under RED Annex II where harmonised standards are applied. There are no EU Safety Gate/RAPEX alerts for the device or the company, and it appears on no market-restriction register in Germany, the Netherlands, Poland, France or Italy. Sold direct into the EU.

Australia - NOT restricted. No ACMA prohibition, no Australian Border Force import prohibition (its 74-item list has no RF multi-tool category), and no state device ban. The device has a registered Australian RCM Supplier's Declaration of Conformity for model FZ.1 dated 2022 - note that is a 2022 declaration citing notices since superseded, so read it as 'has a registered RCM declaration', not 'is currently certified'. Sold locally through resellers. State provisions such as NSW Crimes Act ss.308F/308G/192L and QLD Criminal Code s.408E are intent-gated conduct offences, not device bans. Ignore the widely-syndicated claim that Australia enacted 'unauthorised signal-capture device' rules on 2026-07-01 with AU$55,000 penalties - no such scheme exists and the claim appears to be fabricated.
legal.notes: Owning a Flipper Zero is legal in the US, the UK, the EU and most of the world - the device is CE/FCC marked and sold openly by the vendor. What gets people in trouble is USE, not ownership: transmitting on sub-GHz frequencies you are not licensed for, opening a gate or car that is not yours, cloning an access credential without permission, or interfering with a radio service are separate offences almost everywhere, and they are the offences people actually get charged with. Note also that the community firmwares remove a region lock that exists specifically to keep you inside your national band plan - once you flash one, staying legal is on you. Be careful with the reporting on this device: several widely-repeated 'bans' were proposals that were dropped, marketplace policies, or one-off customs and airport-security incidents rather than law - and at least one site publishes an entirely fabricated Australian restriction that has no basis at all. The real trend to watch is different and newer: legislators have moved away from naming the Flipper and towards banning possession of 'vehicle security circumvention' or 'key fob signal' devices as a CLASS, sometimes without requiring any intent to steal and without exempting researchers. Delaware has such a law in force; the UK has one passed but not yet commenced; Canada has given itself the power to make one. If you own one of these devices, that class-based drafting is what should be on your radar, not the 2024 headlines. Alongside those, most countries already have INTENT-BASED offences that catch misuse without touching ownership: Canada's Criminal Code s.333.2 (in force 2024-07-20, possessing a device suitable for vehicle theft FOR THE PURPOSE of committing it, max 10 years - Justice Canada's own note says that absent intent, possession is not an offence), and in the US 18 U.S.C. 1029 access-device fraud, 18 U.S.C. 1030 (CFAA), 47 U.S.C. 301/302a/333 for unlicensed transmission and interference, and the Wiretap Act. Finally, be sceptical of specific claims: no country has ever enacted a law banning the Flipper Zero BY NAME, and reported bans in Thailand and India trace to unsourced or AI-generated pages with no regulator announcement behind them. Treat this as 'check your own local law', not legal advice.

name: Flipper Zero
firmware_note: The conservative unlock: removes region restrictions and adds a lot of sub-GHz protocol work, while staying close to official firmware and API-compatible with its apps.
price_note: Direct from the vendor, in stock at time of checking. A microSD card is required and is not in the box. Grey-market resellers in countries where import is awkward charge well above this.
skill_note: Behaves almost exactly like stock, so nothing new to learn; the difference is what it will let you transmit.
build_note: Five minutes via the web installer at web.unleashedflip.com. Extra apps come as a separate app pack you copy to the SD card.
summary: A pocket multitool built around four independent radios - a CC1101 sub-GHz transceiver, an ST25R3916 13.56 MHz NFC front end, a separate 125 kHz coil driven straight off the STM32, and the STM32WB55's own Bluetooth LE core - plus infrared, iButton and an 18-pin GPIO header. Unleashed is the most stable and most actively released community fork. It removes the sub-GHz region lock, adds a large number of sub-GHz protocol decoders and manual-creation flows, an on-device frequency analyser and external CC1101 module support, and stays API-compatible with official firmware apps. Extra apps ship separately as an app pack rather than being compiled in.
honest_take: If you want the region lock gone and nothing else weird, this is the one - it is the least opinionated fork and by some distance the most frequently released. It is also where most of the real sub-GHz and NFC engineering in this ecosystem now happens; the other forks pull from it. Do not expect a flashier device: Unleashed deliberately does not ship the animations, theming and joke apps, and BLE Spam is a bundled SD-card app rather than a firmware feature.
best_for: Removing the region lock with the least deviation from stock behaviour
Serious sub-GHz protocol work - this is where most of that engineering happens
People who want frequent, well-tested releases
Driving an external CC1101 module for better range or an amplifier
not_for: Wi-Fi attacks without the ESP32 add-on board
Cracking modern rolling-code car keys
Anyone who wants themes, animations and every app preinstalled - use RogueMaster or Momentum
Transmitting legally without checking your own band plan first

hardware.mcu_primary_note: Dual core: Cortex-M4 @64MHz runs the application, Cortex-M0+ @32MHz runs the BLE stack. Linker script in the firmware confirms 1024K flash; 256KB SRAM total.

radios.note: TI CC1101 transceiver. Silicon is specified by TI for 300-348, 387-464 and 779-928 MHz only - it is NOT continuous 300-928 MHz. Max +12 dBm, OOK/ASK/2-FSK/4-FSK/GFSK/MSK, 0.6-600 kbps. Fixed-function transceiver, not an SDR.
13.56 MHz ONLY. Reader for ISO14443-3A/3B/4A/4B, ISO15693, FeliCa. It has nothing to do with the 125 kHz LF path.

125 kHz has NO dedicated chip. It is a discrete analog front end on its own separate coil, driven by the STM32: TIM1/TIM2 generate the carrier, COMP1 with a 1.2V internal reference demodulates the return. Confirmed in targets/f7/furi_hal/furi_hal_rfid.c.
Bluetooth LE only, on the M0+ coprocessor. There is NO Bluetooth Classic and no Wi-Fi anywhere in this device.
38 kHz IR receiver plus 3 discrete transmit LEDs. Learns and replays consumer IR.

hardware.battery_note: Li-Po. The firmware's fuel-gauge config (targets/f7/furi_hal/furi_hal_power_config.c) programs design capacity 2100 mAh; some spec sheets quote the cell as 2000 mAh nominal. Roughly a week idle, about a day of heavy RF use.
hardware.pmic: TI BQ25896 charger + TI BQ27220 fuel gauge
hardware.storage: microSD up to 256GB. NOT included, and the device is close to useless without one - all saved signals, cards, IR libraries and apps live on it.
hardware.gpio: 18-pin header, 3.3V logic (5V tolerant it is NOT). Exposes UART, SPI, I2C, 1-Wire and SWD. Pin 9 is a switchable 3.3V rail and pin 1 a switchable 5V rail, 1.2A max each, 5W total across the header; each I/O pin sources up to 20mA through a 51 ohm series resistor with ESD protection.

IR window (TSOP-75338 receiver + 3 TX LEDs)
iButton / 1-Wire contact pad on the top edge
18-pin GPIO header
Two separate RFID antennas: a 125 kHz LF coil and a 13.56 MHz HF antenna
No external antenna connector of any kind

subghz_rx.note: 300-348 / 387-464 / 779-928 MHz via CC1101. RX is not region-restricted on any firmware.

subghz_replay.note: Capture and replay works reliably against STATIC-code devices: most older garage doors, gate remotes, barriers, some doorbells and cheap wireless sensors.

subghz_external_antenna.note: The Flipper still has no antenna connector, but community firmware supports an EXTERNAL CC1101 module over GPIO (hardware SPI), and those modules do have SMA connectors and sometimes an amplifier.

subghz_amplified.note: Only via an external amplified CC1101 module on the GPIO header; the internal radio is unchanged.

lf_125khz_read.note: EM4100/EM4102, HID Prox, Indala, IoProx and friends. Reads the ID off the card.

lf_125khz_write.note: Writes only to writable blank fobs (T5577, EM4305). You cannot rewrite a factory EM4100 or a real HID card - those are read-only silicon.

lf_125khz_emulate.note: Emulates saved LF credentials well. This is genuinely one of the things it is best at.

hf_1356_read.note: ISO14443-3A/3B/4A/4B, ISO15693, FeliCa, MIFARE Ultralight/Classic/Plus/DESFire, SLIX, ST25TB. 'Read' means UID plus whatever the card hands over without keys.

hf_1356_write.note: Only to 'magic'/gen1a-gen4 cards with a writable UID, which you have to buy separately. You cannot write a UID onto a normal card.

iso15693.note: Read and emulate ISO15693-3, plus SLIX variants.

felica.note: Reads FeliCa and has a listener, but no key material means Suica-style stored-value cards are read-only curiosities.

mifare_desfire.note: READ ONLY on every firmware. nfc_listener_defs.c has NULL for MfDesfire on official AND on all the community forks - DESFire emulation does not exist. Reading gets you the card's application/file structure and UID, not encrypted file contents, because AES/3DES keys are not recoverable.

ir_tx.note: 3 IR LEDs. Universal remote plus a large community IR database on the SD card.

ir_learn.note: Learns raw and decoded consumer IR protocols.

ir_universal_remote.note: Built in, with community-maintained code sets for TVs, ACs, projectors and audio gear.

ble_advertise.note: The STM32WB55's BLE core can advertise arbitrary payloads, which is what all the 'spam' and tag-emulation apps exploit.

ble_hid.note: Acts as a BLE keyboard/mouse - remote control apps and BLE-based BadUSB.

bt_classic.note: STM32WB55 is Bluetooth LE only. No A2DP, no Classic pairing, no BR/EDR sniffing. A common misconception.

ble_sniff.note: The BLE stack is a connectable peripheral/central stack, not a promiscuous sniffer. It cannot follow connections like an Ubertooth or a Sniffle dongle.

usb_hid_inject.note: BadUSB with Rubber Ducky-compatible scripts. Full-speed USB HID, enumerates as a keyboard.

usb_payload_lang.note: Ducky Script. Large community payload libraries.

uart.note: USB-to-UART bridge and an on-device UART terminal via the GPIO header.

i2c.note: I2C on the GPIO header; community i2ctools app.

jtag_swd.note: SWD only, not JTAG, and via community apps (SWD probe) or the Wi-Fi devboard running Black Magic Probe. Not a first-class debugger.

glitching.note: No fault-injection hardware - no crowbar, no precise clock/voltage glitch path.

ibutton_1wire.note: Reads, writes and emulates Dallas/Cyfral/Metakom iButton keys. Niche outside eastern Europe but works properly.

gps.note: Needs a UART GPS module on the GPIO header.

sd_logging.note: Everything is stored on the microSD card as readable files.

scriptable.note: JavaScript engine (js_app) is built into official firmware and every fork; plus C apps via the SDK.

standalone_untethered.note: Fully self-contained on battery - no phone or laptop required for its core functions.

wifi_scan_24.note: Requires the official Flipper Zero Wi-Fi Dev Board (ESP32-S2) or a third-party ESP32 on the GPIO header. The Flipper itself has no Wi-Fi radio.

wifi_scan_5.note: No firmware or add-on board in this ecosystem does 5 GHz. The official devboard's ESP32-S2 is 2.4 GHz only.

wifi_monitor_mode.note: On the ESP32 add-on, not on the Flipper. Promiscuous mode on ESP32, not true monitor mode with full radiotap.

wifi_deauth_24.note: Runs entirely on an ESP32 add-on flashed with ESP32 Marauder or similar. The Flipper is only a screen, keypad and battery for it.

wifi_evil_twin.note: Evil Portal / Marauder on the ESP32 add-on board.

wifi_captive_portal.note: Evil Portal app drives an ESP32 add-on; the portal HTML lives on the Flipper's SD card.

wifi_handshake_capture.note: ESP32 Marauder on the add-on board. Capture quality is well below a proper Wi-Fi adapter in monitor mode.

wifi_pmkid.note: ESP32 Marauder on the add-on board.

wifi_beacon_spam.note: ESP32 Marauder on the add-on board.

wifi_probe_sniff.note: ESP32 Marauder on the add-on board.

wifi_wardriving.note: Wardriver / Marauder companion apps log WiGLE-format CSV, but need both an ESP32 board and a GPS module on the GPIO header.

nrf24_scan.note: Needs an nRF24L01+ module wired to the GPIO header. Apps exist in the community app packs.

mousejack.note: MouseJacker app plus an nRF24L01+ module on GPIO. Only works against unpatched 2.4 GHz keyboard/mouse dongles, a shrinking target set.

sdr_rx.note: Not an SDR. The CC1101 is a fixed-function narrowband transceiver - you tune it to a frequency and modulation, you do not get IQ samples.

subghz_tx.note: Region lock removed across the CC1101's rated 300-348 / 387-464 / 779-928 MHz bands. A settings file (subghz/assets/setting_user) can add custom frequencies and push beyond the rated range, which the project itself warns can damage the hardware. Legality is on you.

subghz_rolling_code.note: Be precise here. Community firmware lets you SAVE and re-send captured rolling-code signals, and adds manual creation/pairing for protocols like KeeLoq, FAAC SLH, BFT Mitto, Somfy Telis, Nice Flor-S, CAME Atomo and Security+ 2.0 - that is programming a NEW remote into a receiver you control, which needs physical access to the receiver's learn button. It does NOT let you clone someone's rolling-code remote from a captured press. The genuine exception is the RollBack class of attack (Csikor et al., arXiv:2210.11923): replaying two or more consecutively captured codes can roll a receiver's counter back and make old codes valid again. That is implemented openly in the 'rolling_flaws' app and is what the 2025 'DarkWeb firmware' stories were repackaging. Even where it works it only reaches the LOCK/UNLOCK remote-keyless-entry function on some brands - it does NOT touch the immobiliser, so it does not start a car.

subghz_bruteforce.note: Sub-GHz Bruteforcer app included. Only meaningful against short STATIC codes - 8-12 bit DIP-switch style remotes and some fixed-code gates. It will not brute-force a rolling code in any useful timeframe.

mifare_classic_attacks.note: Best-in-class for a device this cheap, but know the boundary. On device: dictionary attack against known keys, and the mfkey32 READER attack (emulate the card at a real reader, harvest nonces, recover Crypto-1 keys in a few minutes). Community firmware also adds card-only nested attack collection. What still generally needs a PC is the heavy maths: hardnested and full nested recovery, where the Flipper collects nonces into a .nested.log and a desktop tool or web service does the cracking. Static nested can be finished on device. Once keys are known it emulates the card and can write to 'magic' cards.

nfc_type4_ndef.note: This is a genuine community-firmware-only capability. The forks add Type4Tag and Ntag4xx protocol modules that official firmware does not have: they READ NTAG 4xx and generic ISO14443-4 Type 4 tags, and there is a Type4Tag LISTENER, so the Flipper can present itself as an NDEF Type 4 tag (this is what the NFC Maker app uses to serve URLs, Wi-Fi credentials, contact cards). Note Ntag4xx itself is read-only - its listener entry is NULL - and DESFire emulation does not exist on any firmware.

emv_read.note: Community firmware has a real EMV poller, so it can read the openly-readable side of a contactless bank card: PAN, expiry, cardholder name where present, and sometimes a transaction log. That is NOT cloning - it cannot produce the dynamic cryptogram a terminal demands, so it cannot pay. Worth knowing: the EMV plugin was silently BROKEN for a long stretch - it shipped as a plugin that never loaded at all - and was only fixed in Unleashed PR #1073, merged 2026-08-20, then flowed downstream. If you used a build from before late August 2026, EMV appeared to be supported but did nothing.

hf_1356_emulate.note: Emulation exists for ISO14443-3A, ISO14443-4A, ISO15693-3, MIFARE Ultralight, MIFARE Classic, MIFARE Plus, SLIX, FeliCa and generic Type 4 Tag. Still NULL and therefore impossible: ISO14443-3B, ISO14443-4B, DESFire, ST25TB, NTAG4xx.

magspoof.note: MagSpoof app is bundled, but it needs an external coil/H-bridge on the GPIO header to actually emit a magstripe field.

usb_mass_storage.note: Mass Storage app bundled - the Flipper presents an SD-card image as a USB drive.

spi_flash_dump.note: SPI Mem Manager app is bundled; you still need test clips/wires to reach the chip.

logic_analyzer.note: Bundled community app. Low sample rate - fine for UART/I2C at modest speeds, not a bench analyser.

findmy_track.note: Read this carefully because the name misleads everyone: FindMy Flipper does NOT find or track other people's AirTags. It turns the Flipper itself INTO a trackable tag, broadcasting a BLE beacon that Apple's Find My network (or Samsung SmartThings / Tile) picks up, so YOU can locate your own Flipper. Setup is either cloning an existing tag's MAC and payload (which requires killing the original tag's battery so it stops rotating keys) or generating OpenHaystack key pairs with Docker/Python on a PC and importing a .keys file. It is an app, not a radio feature - the underlying hardware capability is just 'BLE can advertise'. Unleashed compiles this one in (applications/system/find_my_flipper), as it does the mfkey cracker.

ble_tracker_detect.note: Separate community apps scan for tracker advertisements and match on service UUID / manufacturer data. Not the same thing as FindMy Flipper, and not a firmware feature.

import_restricted: Delaware, USA - THE STRICTEST PROVISION FOUND ANYWHERE, and it is IN FORCE. 21 Del. C. section 6711 (added by 85 Del. Laws c.393, signed 2026-07-23) makes it an offence to knowingly possess, manufacture, sell, transfer or offer a 'vehicle security circumvention device', defined to include 'any other device ... designed or used to intercept the signal from the key fob of a motor vehicle'. Note what is and is not required: you must KNOWINGLY possess the device, but there is NO requirement that you intended to use it to steal a car. The exemption list is closed and covers law enforcement, the National Insurance Crime Bureau, dealers, distributors, manufacturers, mechanics, locksmiths and repossession agents - security researchers and hobbyists are NOT on it. Whether a general-purpose device like a Flipper Zero falls inside that definition is arguable and appears untested, but anyone in Delaware should take advice rather than assume it does not.

United Kingdom - ENACTED BUT NOT YET IN FORCE. Crime and Policing Act 2026 (c.20) section 149, Royal Assent 2026-04-29, creates an offence of possessing, importing, making, adapting or supplying an electronic device 'in circumstances which give rise to a reasonable suspicion that the device will be used in connection with' vehicle theft, with up to 5 years on indictment and a defence the defendant must prove. legislation.gov.uk marks section 149 'Prospective' and none of the commencement orders made so far brings it into force. Some outlets are already reporting it as live law; it is not. Until it is commenced, the Flipper is legal to own and is sold direct into the UK under a UKCA Declaration of Conformity.

Brazil - the only genuine national restriction anywhere, and it is narrower than reported. ANATEL closed the simplified self-declaration homologation route for this product in March 2023, treating it like signal jammers and illicit TV boxes, under Resolution 715/2019 art. 60, II (homologation must be refused where a product serves illicit ends). Certification is compulsory under LGT art. 162 para 2, so uncertified units get held at customs. Three things are commonly got wrong: POSSESSION is not an offence (LGT art. 162 para 2 prohibits use, and Res. 715/2019 art. 83's list of sanctionable conduct omits possession; penalties are administrative); it is NOT established that the manufacturer applied and was refused, as the outlet that reported it published an errata saying users rather than Flipper Devices approached ANATEL; and the much-quoted '340+ seizures' figure is from March 2023 and has never been updated, so it must not be presented as current. Res. 715/2019 art. 88 provides a research/experimental import waiver on paper, but no granted case is documented. Marketplace delistings (Mercado Livre, OLX) were their own terms of service, though Res. 780/2025 has since made marketplaces jointly liable for non-homologated listings.

Canada - the popular story is wrong in BOTH directions. The February 2024 'ban' was indeed withdrawn: ISED announced it on 2024-02-08 and by 2024-03-20 had revised it to restricting use by illegitimate actors. The device is ISED-certified (Technical Acceptance Certificate 27624-FZ) and the vendor lists Canada as 'Direct sale' today. BUT it is not true that nothing was enacted - Bill C-69 (2024, c.17, ss.380-382) amended the Radiocommunication Act to add s.4(5) and s.5.01, in force since 2024-06-20, giving the minister power to specify by order devices whose possession, import and sale are then prohibited, with penalties to $25,000 for individuals and $10,000,000 for corporations. No order has ever been made under s.5.01 and the Flipper Zero has never been specified; the follow-up consultation (Gazette Notice DGSO-003-24, closed August 2024) named seven categories of purpose-built auto-theft tool and did NOT name the Flipper Zero, and produced no decision document. Public Safety's own status page as of May 2025 still records ISED as 'evaluating potential approaches'. The accurate line is 'the power to ban it exists and has sat unused for over two years', not 'nothing happened'.

United States (federal) - NOT restricted. The device holds three FCC Grants of Equipment Authorization under FCC ID 2A2V6-FZ, all dated 2022-01-14, covering 2.4 GHz DTS, Part 15 security/remote control on 304.5-321.95 / 433.075-434.775 / 915-927.95 MHz, and 13.56 MHz. The FCC has never issued an advisory or enforcement action naming it. CBP held a container of about 15,000 units from September to October 2022 and released them roughly a month later with no reason given, and there have been no seizures since. Amazon delisted it on 2023-04-07 as a 'card skimming device' and eBay listings have been blocked since around October 2022, but marketplace policies are not law. It is legal to own and buy federally - but see Delaware above, and expect more states to legislate.

California, USA - IN FORCE but a poor fit. Penal Code s.466, as amended by AB 486 (Ch. 367 of 2025) effective 2026-01-01, adds 'key programming device', 'key duplicating device' and 'signal extender' to the burglary-tools list. Unlike Delaware it REQUIRES intent to feloniously break or enter, and the definitions target devices that access a vehicle's onboard computer or amplify a fob's range - arguably not what a Flipper Zero does. Listed for completeness rather than as a live risk.

European Union - NOT restricted, and legally placed on the market in all 27 member states. Flipper Devices holds an EU Declaration of Conformity under the Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU plus RoHS for model FZ.1, self-declared, which is lawful under RED Annex II where harmonised standards are applied. There are no EU Safety Gate/RAPEX alerts for the device or the company, and it appears on no market-restriction register in Germany, the Netherlands, Poland, France or Italy. Sold direct into the EU.

Australia - NOT restricted. No ACMA prohibition, no Australian Border Force import prohibition (its 74-item list has no RF multi-tool category), and no state device ban. The device has a registered Australian RCM Supplier's Declaration of Conformity for model FZ.1 dated 2022 - note that is a 2022 declaration citing notices since superseded, so read it as 'has a registered RCM declaration', not 'is currently certified'. Sold locally through resellers. State provisions such as NSW Crimes Act ss.308F/308G/192L and QLD Criminal Code s.408E are intent-gated conduct offences, not device bans. Ignore the widely-syndicated claim that Australia enacted 'unauthorised signal-capture device' rules on 2026-07-01 with AU$55,000 penalties - no such scheme exists and the claim appears to be fabricated.
legal.notes: Owning a Flipper Zero is legal in the US, the UK, the EU and most of the world - the device is CE/FCC marked and sold openly by the vendor. What gets people in trouble is USE, not ownership: transmitting on sub-GHz frequencies you are not licensed for, opening a gate or car that is not yours, cloning an access credential without permission, or interfering with a radio service are separate offences almost everywhere, and they are the offences people actually get charged with. Note also that the community firmwares remove a region lock that exists specifically to keep you inside your national band plan - once you flash one, staying legal is on you. Be careful with the reporting on this device: several widely-repeated 'bans' were proposals that were dropped, marketplace policies, or one-off customs and airport-security incidents rather than law - and at least one site publishes an entirely fabricated Australian restriction that has no basis at all. The real trend to watch is different and newer: legislators have moved away from naming the Flipper and towards banning possession of 'vehicle security circumvention' or 'key fob signal' devices as a CLASS, sometimes without requiring any intent to steal and without exempting researchers. Delaware has such a law in force; the UK has one passed but not yet commenced; Canada has given itself the power to make one. If you own one of these devices, that class-based drafting is what should be on your radar, not the 2024 headlines. Alongside those, most countries already have INTENT-BASED offences that catch misuse without touching ownership: Canada's Criminal Code s.333.2 (in force 2024-07-20, possessing a device suitable for vehicle theft FOR THE PURPOSE of committing it, max 10 years - Justice Canada's own note says that absent intent, possession is not an offence), and in the US 18 U.S.C. 1029 access-device fraud, 18 U.S.C. 1030 (CFAA), 47 U.S.C. 301/302a/333 for unlicensed transmission and interference, and the Wiretap Act. Finally, be sceptical of specific claims: no country has ever enacted a law banning the Flipper Zero BY NAME, and reported bans in Thailand and India trace to unsourced or AI-generated pages with no regulator announcement behind them. Treat this as 'check your own local law', not legal advice.

name: Flipper Zero
firmware_note: Kitchen-sink build: takes Unleashed and official upstream and bolts on essentially every community app and game that exists, plus heavy theming.
price_note: Direct from the vendor, in stock at time of checking. A microSD card is required and is not in the box. Grey-market resellers in countries where import is awkward charge well above this.
skill_note: Not because it is technically harder, but because the sheer number of bundled apps - many unmaintained - makes it harder to tell what actually works and what is broken.
build_note: Web installer from rogue-master.net. Bear in mind the very large asset packs slow the device down noticeably.
summary: A pocket multitool built around four independent radios - a CC1101 sub-GHz transceiver, an ST25R3916 13.56 MHz NFC front end, a separate 125 kHz coil driven straight off the STM32, and the STM32WB55's own Bluetooth LE core - plus infrared, iButton and an 18-pin GPIO header. RogueMaster is the maximalist fork: it tracks Unleashed and official upstream and adds nearly every community plugin, game, IR remote and asset pack in existence. Frequent builds, an enormous app list, and a Patreon that gates the most frequent compiled releases (GitHub releases run roughly monthly; the source is open either way).
honest_take: The value here is curation-by-inclusion, not original engineering - almost all the RF and NFC work it ships comes from Unleashed and official upstream, which the changelog is honest about crediting. The cost is real: hundreds of bundled apps of wildly varying quality, large asset packs that make the device sluggish, and a much bigger surface for something to be subtly broken. If you want everything to try and do not mind the mess, it is great. If you want to trust that a feature works, use Unleashed.
best_for: Trying the widest possible range of community apps without hunting them down
Games, themes and general tinkering
Having every IR remote and AC protocol preloaded
not_for: Anyone who wants a lean, predictable device
Wi-Fi attacks without the add-on board
Relying on any given bundled app being maintained

hardware.mcu_primary_note: Dual core: Cortex-M4 @64MHz runs the application, Cortex-M0+ @32MHz runs the BLE stack. Linker script in the firmware confirms 1024K flash; 256KB SRAM total.

radios.note: TI CC1101 transceiver. Silicon is specified by TI for 300-348, 387-464 and 779-928 MHz only - it is NOT continuous 300-928 MHz. Max +12 dBm, OOK/ASK/2-FSK/4-FSK/GFSK/MSK, 0.6-600 kbps. Fixed-function transceiver, not an SDR.
13.56 MHz ONLY. Reader for ISO14443-3A/3B/4A/4B, ISO15693, FeliCa. It has nothing to do with the 125 kHz LF path.

125 kHz has NO dedicated chip. It is a discrete analog front end on its own separate coil, driven by the STM32: TIM1/TIM2 generate the carrier, COMP1 with a 1.2V internal reference demodulates the return. Confirmed in targets/f7/furi_hal/furi_hal_rfid.c.
Bluetooth LE only, on the M0+ coprocessor. There is NO Bluetooth Classic and no Wi-Fi anywhere in this device.
38 kHz IR receiver plus 3 discrete transmit LEDs. Learns and replays consumer IR.

hardware.battery_note: Li-Po. The firmware's fuel-gauge config (targets/f7/furi_hal/furi_hal_power_config.c) programs design capacity 2100 mAh; some spec sheets quote the cell as 2000 mAh nominal. Roughly a week idle, about a day of heavy RF use.
hardware.pmic: TI BQ25896 charger + TI BQ27220 fuel gauge
hardware.storage: microSD up to 256GB. NOT included, and the device is close to useless without one - all saved signals, cards, IR libraries and apps live on it.
hardware.gpio: 18-pin header, 3.3V logic (5V tolerant it is NOT). Exposes UART, SPI, I2C, 1-Wire and SWD. Pin 9 is a switchable 3.3V rail and pin 1 a switchable 5V rail, 1.2A max each, 5W total across the header; each I/O pin sources up to 20mA through a 51 ohm series resistor with ESD protection.

IR window (TSOP-75338 receiver + 3 TX LEDs)

ble_hid.note: Acts as a BLE keyboard/mouse - remote control apps and BLE-based BadUSB.

bt_classic.note: STM32WB55 is Bluetooth LE only. No A2DP, no Classic pairing, no BR/EDR sniffing. A common misconception.

subghz_rolling_code.note: Be precise here. Community firmware lets you SAVE and re-send captured rolling-code signals, and adds manual creation/pairing for protocols like KeeLoq, FAAC SLH, BFT Mitto, Somfy Telis, Nice Flor-S, CAME Atomo and Security+ 2.0 - that is programming a NEW remote into a receiver you control, which needs physical access to the receiver's learn button. It does NOT let you clone someone's rolling-code remote from a captured press. The genuine exception is the RollBack class of attack (Csikor et al., arXiv:2210.11923): replaying two or more consecutively captured codes can roll a receiver's counter back and make old codes valid again. That is implemented openly in the 'rolling_flaws' app and is what the 2025 'DarkWeb firmware' stories were repackaging. Even where it works it only reaches the LOCK/UNLOCK remote-keyless-entry function on some brands - it does NOT touch the immobiliser, so it does not start a car.

subghz_bruteforce.note: Sub-GHz Bruteforcer app included. Only meaningful against short STATIC codes - 8-12 bit DIP-switch style remotes and some fixed-code gates. It will not brute-force a rolling code in any useful timeframe.

mifare_classic_attacks.note: Best-in-class for a device this cheap, but know the boundary. On device: dictionary attack against known keys, and the mfkey32 READER attack (emulate the card at a real reader, harvest nonces, recover Crypto-1 keys in a few minutes). Community firmware also adds card-only nested attack collection. What still generally needs a PC is the heavy maths: hardnested and full nested recovery, where the Flipper collects nonces into a .nested.log and a desktop tool or web service does the cracking. Static nested can be finished on device. Once keys are known it emulates the card and can write to 'magic' cards.
