import_restricted: Delaware, USA - THE STRICTEST PROVISION FOUND ANYWHERE, and it is IN FORCE. 21 Del. C. section 6711 (added by 85 Del. Laws c.393, signed 2026-07-23) makes it an offence to knowingly possess, manufacture, sell, transfer or offer a 'vehicle security circumvention device', defined to include 'any other device ... designed or used to intercept the signal from the key fob of a motor vehicle'. Note what is and is not required: you must KNOWINGLY possess the device, but there is NO requirement that you intended to use it to steal a car. The exemption list is closed and covers law enforcement, the National Insurance Crime Bureau, dealers, distributors, manufacturers, mechanics, locksmiths and repossession agents - security researchers and hobbyists are NOT on it. Whether a general-purpose device like a Flipper Zero falls inside that definition is arguable and appears untested, but anyone in Delaware should take advice rather than assume it does not.

United Kingdom - ENACTED BUT NOT YET IN FORCE. Crime and Policing Act 2026 (c.20) section 149, Royal Assent 2026-04-29, creates an offence of possessing, importing, making, adapting or supplying an electronic device 'in circumstances which give rise to a reasonable suspicion that the device will be used in connection with' vehicle theft, with up to 5 years on indictment and a defence the defendant must prove. legislation.gov.uk marks section 149 'Prospective' and none of the commencement orders made so far brings it into force. Some outlets are already reporting it as live law; it is not. Until it is commenced, the Flipper is legal to own and is sold direct into the UK under a UKCA Declaration of Conformity.

Brazil - the only genuine national restriction anywhere, and it is narrower than reported. ANATEL closed the simplified self-declaration homologation route for this product in March 2023, treating it like signal jammers and illicit TV boxes, under Resolution 715/2019 art. 60, II (homologation must be refused where a product serves illicit ends). Certification is compulsory under LGT art. 162 para 2, so uncertified units get held at customs. Three things are commonly got wrong: POSSESSION is not an offence (LGT art. 162 para 2 prohibits use, and Res. 715/2019 art. 83's list of sanctionable conduct omits possession; penalties are administrative); it is NOT established that the manufacturer applied and was refused, as the outlet that reported it published an errata saying users rather than Flipper Devices approached ANATEL; and the much-quoted '340+ seizures' figure is from March 2023 and has never been updated, so it must not be presented as current. Res. 715/2019 art. 88 provides a research/experimental import waiver on paper, but no granted case is documented. Marketplace delistings (Mercado Livre, OLX) were their own terms of service, though Res. 780/2025 has since made marketplaces jointly liable for non-homologated listings.

Canada - the popular story is wrong in BOTH directions. The February 2024 'ban' was indeed withdrawn: ISED announced it on 2024-02-08 and by 2024-03-20 had revised it to restricting use by illegitimate actors. The device is ISED-certified (Technical Acceptance Certificate 27624-FZ) and the vendor lists Canada as 'Direct sale' today. BUT it is not true that nothing was enacted - Bill C-69 (2024, c.17, ss.380-382) amended the Radiocommunication Act to add s.4(5) and s.5.01, in force since 2024-06-20, giving the minister power to specify by order devices whose possession, import and sale are then prohibited, with penalties to $25,000 for individuals and $10,000,000 for corporations. No order has ever been made under s.5.01 and the Flipper Zero has never been specified; the follow-up consultation (Gazette Notice DGSO-003-24, closed August 2024) named seven categories of purpose-built auto-theft tool and did NOT name the Flipper Zero, and produced no decision document. Public Safety's own status page as of May 2025 still records ISED as 'evaluating potential approaches'. The accurate line is 'the power to ban it exists and has sat unused for over two years', not 'nothing happened'.

United States (federal) - NOT restricted. The device holds three FCC Grants of Equipment Authorization under FCC ID 2A2V6-FZ, all dated 2022-01-14, covering 2.4 GHz DTS, Part 15 security/remote control on 304.5-321.95 / 433.075-434.775 / 915-927.95 MHz, and 13.56 MHz. The FCC has never issued an advisory or enforcement action naming it. CBP held a container of about 15,000 units from September to October 2022 and released them roughly a month later with no reason given, and there have been no seizures since. Amazon delisted it on 2023-04-07 as a 'card skimming device' and eBay listings have been blocked since around October 2022, but marketplace policies are not law. It is legal to own and buy federally - but see Delaware above, and expect more states to legislate.

California, USA - IN FORCE but a poor fit. Penal Code s.466, as amended by AB 486 (Ch. 367 of 2025) effective 2026-01-01, adds 'key programming device', 'key duplicating device' and 'signal extender' to the burglary-tools list. Unlike Delaware it REQUIRES intent to feloniously break or enter, and the definitions target devices that access a vehicle's onboard computer or amplify a fob's range - arguably not what a Flipper Zero does. Listed for completeness rather than as a live risk.

European Union - NOT restricted, and legally placed on the market in all 27 member states. Flipper Devices holds an EU Declaration of Conformity under the Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU plus RoHS for model FZ.1, self-declared, which is lawful under RED Annex II where harmonised standards are applied. There are no EU Safety Gate/RAPEX alerts for the device or the company, and it appears on no market-restriction register in Germany, the Netherlands, Poland, France or Italy. Sold direct into the EU.

Australia - NOT restricted. No ACMA prohibition, no Australian Border Force import prohibition (its 74-item list has no RF multi-tool category), and no state device ban. The device has a registered Australian RCM Supplier's Declaration of Conformity for model FZ.1 dated 2022 - note that is a 2022 declaration citing notices since superseded, so read it as 'has a registered RCM declaration', not 'is currently certified'. Sold locally through resellers. State provisions such as NSW Crimes Act ss.308F/308G/192L and QLD Criminal Code s.408E are intent-gated conduct offences, not device bans. Ignore the widely-syndicated claim that Australia enacted 'unauthorised signal-capture device' rules on 2026-07-01 with AU$55,000 penalties - no such scheme exists and the claim appears to be fabricated.
legal.notes: Owning a Flipper Zero is legal in the US, the UK, the EU and most of the world - the device is CE/FCC marked and sold openly by the vendor. What gets people in trouble is USE, not ownership: transmitting on sub-GHz frequencies you are not licensed for, opening a gate or car that is not yours, cloning an access credential without permission, or interfering with a radio service are separate offences almost everywhere, and they are the offences people actually get charged with. Note also that the community firmwares remove a region lock that exists specifically to keep you inside your national band plan - once you flash one, staying legal is on you. Be careful with the reporting on this device: several widely-repeated 'bans' were proposals that were dropped, marketplace policies, or one-off customs and airport-security incidents rather than law - and at least one site publishes an entirely fabricated Australian restriction that has no basis at all. The real trend to watch is different and newer: legislators have moved away from naming the Flipper and towards banning possession of 'vehicle security circumvention' or 'key fob signal' devices as a CLASS, sometimes without requiring any intent to steal and without exempting researchers. Delaware has such a law in force; the UK has one passed but not yet commenced; Canada has given itself the power to make one. If you own one of these devices, that class-based drafting is what should be on your radar, not the 2024 headlines. Alongside those, most countries already have INTENT-BASED offences that catch misuse without touching ownership: Canada's Criminal Code s.333.2 (in force 2024-07-20, possessing a device suitable for vehicle theft FOR THE PURPOSE of committing it, max 10 years - Justice Canada's own note says that absent intent, possession is not an offence), and in the US 18 U.S.C. 1029 access-device fraud, 18 U.S.C. 1030 (CFAA), 47 U.S.C. 301/302a/333 for unlicensed transmission and interference, and the Wiretap Act. Finally, be sceptical of specific claims: no country has ever enacted a law banning the Flipper Zero BY NAME, and reported bans in Thailand and India trace to unsourced or AI-generated pages with no regulator announcement behind them. Treat this as 'check your own local law', not legal advice.

radios.note: TI CC1101 transceiver. Silicon is specified by TI for 300-348, 387-464 and 779-928 MHz only - it is NOT continuous 300-928 MHz. Max +12 dBm, OOK/ASK/2-FSK/4-FSK/GFSK/MSK, 0.6-600 kbps. Fixed-function transceiver, not an SDR.
13.56 MHz ONLY. Reader for ISO14443-3A/3B/4A/4B, ISO15693, FeliCa. It has nothing to do with the 125 kHz LF path.

lf_125khz_emulate.note: Emulates saved LF credentials well. This is genuinely one of the things it is best at.

hf_1356_read.note: ISO14443-3A/3B/4A/4B, ISO15693, FeliCa, MIFARE Ultralight/Classic/Plus/DESFire, SLIX, ST25TB. 'Read' means UID plus whatever the card hands over without keys.

hf_1356_write.note: Only to 'magic'/gen1a-gen4 cards with a writable UID, which you have to buy separately. You cannot write a UID onto a normal card.

iso15693.note: Read and emulate ISO15693-3, plus SLIX variants.

felica.note: Reads FeliCa and has a listener, but no key material means Suica-style stored-value cards are read-only curiosities.

mifare_desfire.note: READ ONLY on every firmware. nfc_listener_defs.c has NULL for MfDesfire on official AND on all the community forks - DESFire emulation does not exist. Reading gets you the card's application/file structure and UID, not encrypted file contents, because AES/3DES keys are not recoverable.

ir_tx.note: 3 IR LEDs. Universal remote plus a large community IR database on the SD card.

ir_learn.note: Learns raw and decoded consumer IR protocols.

ir_universal_remote.note: Built in, with community-maintained code sets for TVs, ACs, projectors and audio gear.

ble_advertise.note: The STM32WB55's BLE core can advertise arbitrary payloads, which is what all the 'spam' and tag-emulation apps exploit.

ble_hid.note: Acts as a BLE keyboard/mouse - remote control apps and BLE-based BadUSB.

bt_classic.note: STM32WB55 is Bluetooth LE only. No A2DP, no Classic pairing, no BR/EDR sniffing. A common misconception.

ble_sniff.note: The BLE stack is a connectable peripheral/central stack, not a promiscuous sniffer. It cannot follow connections like an Ubertooth or a Sniffle dongle.

usb_hid_inject.note: BadUSB with Rubber Ducky-compatible scripts. Full-speed USB HID, enumerates as a keyboard.

usb_payload_lang.note: Ducky Script. Large community payload libraries.

uart.note: USB-to-UART bridge and an on-device UART terminal via the GPIO header.

i2c.note: I2C on the GPIO header; community i2ctools app.

jtag_swd.note: SWD only, not JTAG, and via community apps (SWD probe) or the Wi-Fi devboard running Black Magic Probe. Not a first-class debugger.

glitching.note: No fault-injection hardware - no crowbar, no precise clock/voltage glitch path.

ibutton_1wire.note: Reads, writes and emulates Dallas/Cyfral/Metakom iButton keys. Niche outside eastern Europe but works properly.

gps.note: Needs a UART GPS module on the GPIO header.

sd_logging.note: Everything is stored on the microSD card as readable files.

scriptable.note: JavaScript engine (js_app) is built into official firmware and every fork; plus C apps via the SDK.

standalone_untethered.note: Fully self-contained on battery - no phone or laptop required for its core functions.

wifi_scan_24.note: Requires the official Flipper Zero Wi-Fi Dev Board (ESP32-S2) or a third-party ESP32 on the GPIO header. The Flipper itself has no Wi-Fi radio.

wifi_scan_5.note: No firmware or add-on board in this ecosystem does 5 GHz. The official devboard's ESP32-S2 is 2.4 GHz only.

wifi_monitor_mode.note: On the ESP32 add-on, not on the Flipper. Promiscuous mode on ESP32, not true monitor mode with full radiotap.

wifi_deauth_24.note: Runs entirely on an ESP32 add-on flashed with ESP32 Marauder or similar. The Flipper is only a screen, keypad and battery for it.

wifi_evil_twin.note: Evil Portal / Marauder on the ESP32 add-on board.

wifi_captive_portal.note: Evil Portal app drives an ESP32 add-on; the portal HTML lives on the Flipper's SD card.

wifi_handshake_capture.note: ESP32 Marauder on the add-on board. Capture quality is well below a proper Wi-Fi adapter in monitor mode.

wifi_pmkid.note: ESP32 Marauder on the add-on board.

wifi_beacon_spam.note: ESP32 Marauder on the add-on board.

wifi_probe_sniff.note: ESP32 Marauder on the add-on board.

wifi_wardriving.note: Wardriver / Marauder companion apps log WiGLE-format CSV, but need both an ESP32 board and a GPS module on the GPIO header.

nrf24_scan.note: Needs an nRF24L01+ module wired to the GPIO header. Apps exist in the community app packs.

mousejack.note: MouseJacker app plus an nRF24L01+ module on GPIO. Only works against unpatched 2.4 GHz keyboard/mouse dongles, a shrinking target set.

sdr_rx.note: Not an SDR. The CC1101 is a fixed-function narrowband transceiver - you tune it to a frequency and modulation, you do not get IQ samples.

subghz_tx.note: Region lock was removed, within the CC1101's rated bands. Historical - as of the final 2024 release.

subghz_rolling_code.note: Be precise here. Community firmware lets you SAVE and re-send captured rolling-code signals, and adds manual creation/pairing for protocols like KeeLoq, FAAC SLH, BFT Mitto, Somfy Telis, Nice Flor-S, CAME Atomo and Security+ 2.0 - that is programming a NEW remote into a receiver you control, which needs physical access to the receiver's learn button. It does NOT let you clone someone's rolling-code remote from a captured press. The genuine exception is the RollBack class of attack (Csikor et al., arXiv:2210.11923): replaying two or more consecutively captured codes can roll a receiver's counter back and make old codes valid again. That is implemented openly in the 'rolling_flaws' app and is what the 2025 'DarkWeb firmware' stories were repackaging. Even where it works it only reaches the LOCK/UNLOCK remote-keyless-entry function on some brands - it does NOT touch the immobiliser, so it does not start a car.

subghz_bruteforce.note: Sub-GHz Bruteforcer app included. Only meaningful against short STATIC codes - 8-12 bit DIP-switch style remotes and some fixed-code gates. It will not brute-force a rolling code in any useful timeframe.

mifare_classic_attacks.note: Best-in-class for a device this cheap, but know the boundary. On device: dictionary attack against known keys, and the mfkey32 READER attack (emulate the card at a real reader, harvest nonces, recover Crypto-1 keys in a few minutes). Community firmware also adds card-only nested attack collection. What still generally needs a PC is the heavy maths: hardnested and full nested recovery, where the Flipper collects nonces into a .nested.log and a desktop tool or web service does the cracking. Static nested can be finished on device. Once keys are known it emulates the card and can write to 'magic' cards.

nfc_type4_ndef.note: This is a genuine community-firmware-only capability. The forks add Type4Tag and Ntag4xx protocol modules that official firmware does not have: they READ NTAG 4xx and generic ISO14443-4 Type 4 tags, and there is a Type4Tag LISTENER, so the Flipper can present itself as an NDEF Type 4 tag (this is what the NFC Maker app uses to serve URLs, Wi-Fi credentials, contact cards). Note Ntag4xx itself is read-only - its listener entry is NULL - and DESFire emulation does not exist on any firmware.

emv_read.note: Could not verify the state of the EMV poller in the final 2024 build. The EMV plugin was broken across the community forks for a long period and was only fixed in August 2026, well after Xtreme was archived - so on Xtreme it is at best unverified and quite possibly non-functional.

hf_1356_emulate.note: Emulation exists for ISO14443-3A, ISO14443-4A, ISO15693-3, MIFARE Ultralight, MIFARE Classic, MIFARE Plus, SLIX, FeliCa and generic Type 4 Tag. Still NULL and therefore impossible: ISO14443-3B, ISO14443-4B, DESFire, ST25TB, NTAG4xx.

magspoof.note: MagSpoof app is bundled, but it needs an external coil/H-bridge on the GPIO header to actually emit a magstripe field.

usb_mass_storage.note: Mass Storage app bundled - the Flipper presents an SD-card image as a USB drive.

spi_flash_dump.note: SPI Mem Manager app is bundled; you still need test clips/wires to reach the chip.

logic_analyzer.note: Bundled community app. Low sample rate - fine for UART/I2C at modest speeds, not a bench analyser.

ble_scan.note: Community BLE scanner/tracker-detector apps exist in the app packs; not a core firmware feature.

ble_spam_apple.note: Apple Continuity. BLE Spam ORIGINATED in Xtreme before moving to Momentum. Historical: as of the 2024 release, and largely mitigated by vendors since. Real, but oversold. The STM32WB55 BLE stack advertises one payload at a time and cycles through them, so this is protocol-level nuisance advertising, not RF jamming and not a flood. Apple (iOS 17.2+), Google, Microsoft and Samsung all added cooldowns and sanity checks after 2023, so on current phones it is mostly a party trick. The app's own author describes it that way.

import_restricted: Delaware, USA - THE STRICTEST PROVISION FOUND ANYWHERE, and it is IN FORCE. 21 Del. C. section 6711 (added by 85 Del. Laws c.393, signed 2026-07-23) makes it an offence to knowingly possess, manufacture, sell, transfer or offer a 'vehicle security circumvention device', defined to include 'any other device ... designed or used to intercept the signal from the key fob of a motor vehicle'. Note what is and is not required: you must KNOWINGLY possess the device, but there is NO requirement that you intended to use it to steal a car. The exemption list is closed and covers law enforcement, the National Insurance Crime Bureau, dealers, distributors, manufacturers, mechanics, locksmiths and repossession agents - security researchers and hobbyists are NOT on it. Whether a general-purpose device like a Flipper Zero falls inside that definition is arguable and appears untested, but anyone in Delaware should take advice rather than assume it does not.

United Kingdom - ENACTED BUT NOT YET IN FORCE. Crime and Policing Act 2026 (c.20) section 149, Royal Assent 2026-04-29, creates an offence of possessing, importing, making, adapting or supplying an electronic device 'in circumstances which give rise to a reasonable suspicion that the device will be used in connection with' vehicle theft, with up to 5 years on indictment and a defence the defendant must prove. legislation.gov.uk marks section 149 'Prospective' and none of the commencement orders made so far brings it into force. Some outlets are already reporting it as live law; it is not. Until it is commenced, the Flipper is legal to own and is sold direct into the UK under a UKCA Declaration of Conformity.

Brazil - the only genuine national restriction anywhere, and it is narrower than reported. ANATEL closed the simplified self-declaration homologation route for this product in March 2023, treating it like signal jammers and illicit TV boxes, under Resolution 715/2019 art. 60, II (homologation must be refused where a product serves illicit ends). Certification is compulsory under LGT art. 162 para 2, so uncertified units get held at customs. Three things are commonly got wrong: POSSESSION is not an offence (LGT art. 162 para 2 prohibits use, and Res. 715/2019 art. 83's list of sanctionable conduct omits possession; penalties are administrative); it is NOT established that the manufacturer applied and was refused, as the outlet that reported it published an errata saying users rather than Flipper Devices approached ANATEL; and the much-quoted '340+ seizures' figure is from March 2023 and has never been updated, so it must not be presented as current. Res. 715/2019 art. 88 provides a research/experimental import waiver on paper, but no granted case is documented. Marketplace delistings (Mercado Livre, OLX) were their own terms of service, though Res. 780/2025 has since made marketplaces jointly liable for non-homologated listings.

Canada - the popular story is wrong in BOTH directions. The February 2024 'ban' was indeed withdrawn: ISED announced it on 2024-02-08 and by 2024-03-20 had revised it to restricting use by illegitimate actors. The device is ISED-certified (Technical Acceptance Certificate 27624-FZ) and the vendor lists Canada as 'Direct sale' today. BUT it is not true that nothing was enacted - Bill C-69 (2024, c.17, ss.380-382) amended the Radiocommunication Act to add s.4(5) and s.5.01, in force since 2024-06-20, giving the minister power to specify by order devices whose possession, import and sale are then prohibited, with penalties to $25,000 for individuals and $10,000,000 for corporations. No order has ever been made under s.5.01 and the Flipper Zero has never been specified; the follow-up consultation (Gazette Notice DGSO-003-24, closed August 2024) named seven categories of purpose-built auto-theft tool and did NOT name the Flipper Zero, and produced no decision document. Public Safety's own status page as of May 2025 still records ISED as 'evaluating potential approaches'. The accurate line is 'the power to ban it exists and has sat unused for over two years', not 'nothing happened'.

United States (federal) - NOT restricted. The device holds three FCC Grants of Equipment Authorization under FCC ID 2A2V6-FZ, all dated 2022-01-14, covering 2.4 GHz DTS, Part 15 security/remote control on 304.5-321.95 / 433.075-434.775 / 915-927.95 MHz, and 13.56 MHz. The FCC has never issued an advisory or enforcement action naming it. CBP held a container of about 15,000 units from September to October 2022 and released them roughly a month later with no reason given, and there have been no seizures since. Amazon delisted it on 2023-04-07 as a 'card skimming device' and eBay listings have been blocked since around October 2022, but marketplace policies are not law. It is legal to own and buy federally - but see Delaware above, and expect more states to legislate.

California, USA - IN FORCE but a poor fit. Penal Code s.466, as amended by AB 486 (Ch. 367 of 2025) effective 2026-01-01, adds 'key programming device', 'key duplicating device' and 'signal extender' to the burglary-tools list. Unlike Delaware it REQUIRES intent to feloniously break or enter, and the definitions target devices that access a vehicle's onboard computer or amplify a fob's range - arguably not what a Flipper Zero does. Listed for completeness rather than as a live risk.

European Union - NOT restricted, and legally placed on the market in all 27 member states. Flipper Devices holds an EU Declaration of Conformity under the Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU plus RoHS for model FZ.1, self-declared, which is lawful under RED Annex II where harmonised standards are applied. There are no EU Safety Gate/RAPEX alerts for the device or the company, and it appears on no market-restriction register in Germany, the Netherlands, Poland, France or Italy. Sold direct into the EU.

Australia - NOT restricted. No ACMA prohibition, no Australian Border Force import prohibition (its 74-item list has no RF multi-tool category), and no state device ban. The device has a registered Australian RCM Supplier's Declaration of Conformity for model FZ.1 dated 2022 - note that is a 2022 declaration citing notices since superseded, so read it as 'has a registered RCM declaration', not 'is currently certified'. Sold locally through resellers. State provisions such as NSW Crimes Act ss.308F/308G/192L and QLD Criminal Code s.408E are intent-gated conduct offences, not device bans. Ignore the widely-syndicated claim that Australia enacted 'unauthorised signal-capture device' rules on 2026-07-01 with AU$55,000 penalties - no such scheme exists and the claim appears to be fabricated.
legal.notes: Owning a Flipper Zero is legal in the US, the UK, the EU and most of the world - the device is CE/FCC marked and sold openly by the vendor. What gets people in trouble is USE, not ownership: transmitting on sub-GHz frequencies you are not licensed for, opening a gate or car that is not yours, cloning an access credential without permission, or interfering with a radio service are separate offences almost everywhere, and they are the offences people actually get charged with. Note also that the community firmwares remove a region lock that exists specifically to keep you inside your national band plan - once you flash one, staying legal is on you. Be careful with the reporting on this device: several widely-repeated 'bans' were proposals that were dropped, marketplace policies, or one-off customs and airport-security incidents rather than law - and at least one site publishes an entirely fabricated Australian restriction that has no basis at all. The real trend to watch is different and newer: legislators have moved away from naming the Flipper and towards banning possession of 'vehicle security circumvention' or 'key fob signal' devices as a CLASS, sometimes without requiring any intent to steal and without exempting researchers. Delaware has such a law in force; the UK has one passed but not yet commenced; Canada has given itself the power to make one. If you own one of these devices, that class-based drafting is what should be on your radar, not the 2024 headlines. Alongside those, most countries already have INTENT-BASED offences that catch misuse without touching ownership: Canada's Criminal Code s.333.2 (in force 2024-07-20, possessing a device suitable for vehicle theft FOR THE PURPOSE of committing it, max 10 years - Justice Canada's own note says that absent intent, possession is not an offence), and in the US 18 U.S.C. 1029 access-device fraud, 18 U.S.C. 1030 (CFAA), 47 U.S.C. 301/302a/333 for unlicensed transmission and interference, and the Wiretap Act. Finally, be sceptical of specific claims: no country has ever enacted a law banning the Flipper Zero BY NAME, and reported bans in Thailand and India trace to unsourced or AI-generated pages with no regulator announcement behind them. Treat this as 'check your own local law', not legal advice.

name: Flipper Zero Wi-Fi Dev Board
firmware_note: Stock firmware is a DEBUGGER, not an attack tool: SWD over Wi-Fi or USB, plus UART log capture. Offensive Wi-Fi means reflashing it with ESP32 Marauder or GhostESP.
price_note: Listed at $35 (SKU FLP-M-WIFI) but the product page reports OutOfStock and renders a 'Sold out' button. Compounding that, the ESP32-S2-WROVER module it is built on is marked End-of-Life by Espressif, so it may not return in this form. Third-party clones cost the same or less.
skill_note: Plugging it in is trivial; getting offensive Wi-Fi out of it means flashing third-party firmware and knowing what a deauth frame is and when sending one is legal.
build_note: No soldering - it presses onto the 18-pin GPIO header. Power the Flipper OFF first: the official docs warn that hot-plugging a module sharing the 3.3V rail can corrupt the microSD card.
summary: A small ESP32-S2-WROVER board that presses onto the Flipper's GPIO header and gives it the Wi-Fi radio it does not otherwise have. Flipper's own firmware for it is a debug probe - Black Magic Probe SWD over Wi-Fi or USB, DAPLink over USB, and UART log capture that works even when the Flipper's OS is down. The Wi-Fi attack features everyone buys it for come from reflashing it with third-party firmware such as ESP32 Marauder.
honest_take: Two things to get straight. First, this board is where every 'Flipper Zero Wi-Fi hack' video actually happens - the Flipper is just a screen, keypad and battery; the ESP32 does all of it, and you could flash the same Marauder firmware onto a $10 ESP32 dev board. Second, and less well known: the ESP32-S2 has NO Bluetooth radio at all, so Marauder's BLE features - blespam, findmy, sniffbt, Flipper-detection - are compiled out and silently do nothing on this board. It is also single-core, 2.4 GHz only, and the module is EOL at Espressif. Third-party ESP32/ESP32-S3 boards in the same form factor cost about the same and keep Bluetooth. The official board's one real advantage is the thing the clones mostly skip: SWD debugging over Wi-Fi.
best_for: Adding 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi scanning and attacks to a Flipper via Marauder or GhostESP
Wireless SWD debugging of other embedded targets (Black Magic Probe)
Reading Flipper boot/crash logs over UART when the OS itself is broken

not_for: Anything Bluetooth - the ESP32-S2 has no BT radio whatsoever
5 GHz networks - 2.4 GHz only

hardware.mcu_primary_note: Single-core Xtensa LX7 up to 240MHz, 320KB SRAM, 4MB SPI flash + 2MB PSRAM, native full-speed USB OTG (which is why it does USB CDC/DAP with no bridge chip). Marked End-of-Life by Espressif on datasheet v1.4.

radios.note: 802.11 b/g/n, 2412-2484 MHz. 2.4 GHz ONLY - no 802.11a/ac and no 5 GHz anywhere in the datasheet. NO Bluetooth: the ESP32-S2 silicon has no BT block at all.

hardware.battery_note: No battery - powered from the Flipper's 3.3V rail or its own USB-C port. Module datasheet draw at 3.3V is 298-340mA TX / 81-88mA RX, so sustained scanning is a heavy load on the Flipper's cell.
hardware.charging: USB-C (data + power, direct to the ESP32)
hardware.storage: 4MB flash + 2MB PSRAM on-module; microSD only if you wire one to the header yourself
hardware.gpio: Mates with the Flipper's 18-pin header; taps SWDIO/SWCLK plus both UARTs (USART and LPUART). Broken-out ESP IO for SD card and GPS.
notable_physical: On-board PCB antenna (no u.FL on this SKU)
BOOT and RESET tactile switches
Status LEDs
USB-C port wired straight to the ESP32

ble_scan.note: ESP32-S2 has no Bluetooth radio. Marauder's HAS_BT block is commented out for this target, so blespam, findmy, sniffbt, spoofat and sniffskim parse but do nothing.

ble_spam_apple.note: No Bluetooth radio on the ESP32-S2.

jtag_swd.note: This is the board's official purpose: Black Magic Probe SWD over Wi-Fi or USB, and DAPLink/CMSIS-DAP over USB. Documented limitation - Black Magic mode does not support RTOS threads.

uart.note: Reads the Flipper's UART logs independently of the Flipper OS, so boot, update and crash logs survive an unbootable device. USB only for now.

web_ui.note: The ESP32 serves its own web interface, which is how you switch between Black Magic and DAPLink modes.

gps.note: GPS support is compiled into the Marauder build, but the module is not included - you wire it to the header.

sd_logging.note: SD support is compiled in; no card slot on the board.

legal.notes: The board itself is an unremarkable ESP32 development board and is not restricted anywhere we could find - it is the Flipper it attaches to that attracts import attention, not this. The risk is entirely in what you flash onto it and where you point it: sending deauthentication frames at networks you do not own or have written authorisation to test is illegal in most jurisdictions, and in the US the FCC has issued multi-million-dollar fines to hotels and venues for Wi-Fi deauth quite separately from computer-misuse law. Running a captive portal that harvests credentials is a further offence again. Check your own local law.

name: Flipper Zero Video Game Module
firmware_note: Mirrors the Flipper's 128x64 screen to a monitor as 640x480p60 DVI-D, reads the on-board IMU, and exposes a small CLI. That is all it does.
price_note: $49 (SKU FLP-M-VGM), in stock at time of checking. Note the shop URL that circulates in third-party articles (/products/video-game-module) is a 404 - the live handle is /products/video-game-module-for-flipper-zero, which is probably why people assume it was discontinued. It was not.
skill_note: Trivial to plug in and mirror the screen; writing your own firmware means the Raspberry Pi Pico SDK and C.
build_note: Presses onto the GPIO header, no soldering. Custom firmware is UF2 drag-and-drop over USB-C, or flashable from the Flipper itself using the Video Game Module Tool app with no PC at all.
summary: An RP2040 board that presses onto the Flipper's GPIO header, outputs 640x480p60 video over an HDMI-shaped connector, and carries a 6-axis motion sensor for tilt-controlled games. Developed with Raspberry Pi and announced February 2024. It is a genuinely open, Pico-compatible dev board: schematics are published, the toolchain is the standard Pico SDK, and it exposes 11 spare GPIO.
honest_take: Be clear that this is a games and development accessory, not a security tool - there is nothing offensive in the design and nobody has built anything offensive on it. Two technical points worth knowing: the video is DVI-D bit-banged by the RP2040's PIO units via PicoDVI with no transmitter chip, which only works because the chip is overclocked to 252MHz at raised core voltage (1.2V) against a 133MHz rated spec; and Flipper carefully avoid the word HDMI because they have no adopter licence. The bigger problem is that the ecosystem stalled: the official firmware has not been touched since May 2024, the game engine meant to seed it has been untouched since February 2024, and about 1% of the official app catalog targets it. At $49 you are paying roughly ten times a bare Raspberry Pi Pico for the same RP2040, plus a video connector, an IMU and a Flipper-shaped case.
best_for: Playing Flipper games on a monitor and using tilt controls
Using the Flipper as a host for ordinary Raspberry Pi Pico projects, including as a USB oscilloscope
Getting a second, independently programmable MCU with 11 spare GPIO onto a Flipper
not_for: Any security or offensive capability - it adds none
Anyone who just wants an RP2040, which costs about $4 as a bare Pico
Relying on an active software ecosystem - it has largely stalled

hardware.mcu_primary_note: Dual Cortex-M0+, rated 133MHz. The shipped firmware over-volts to 1.2V and sets the clock to 252MHz - roughly 1.9x rated - because generating DVI in software needs it. Core 1 does nothing but drive the scanline buffer.

display.type: Video OUTPUT only (DVI-D over an HDMI-type connector)

hardware.battery_note: No battery. Powered over its own USB-C (5V) or from the Flipper's 3.3V/5V rails.
hardware.charging: USB-C (wired directly to the RP2040; no USB-PD)
hardware.storage: On-board flash for the RP2040 firmware; no card slot
hardware.gpio: 14-pin breakout = 11 ESD-protected GPIO (RP2040 16, 17, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29) + 2 GND + 3.3V. GPIO 8-15 and 18-20 are consumed internally by the video output. Pins 23/24/25/29 are used internally on a real Pico but are free here.
sensors: ICM-42688-P 6-axis IMU (3-axis gyro + 3-axis accelerometer, SPI, up to 32kHz ODR). No magnetometer, so no absolute heading.
notable_physical: HDMI-type connector carrying DVI-D (DDC SDA/SCL and CEC are wired)
BOOT and RESET buttons (need a paper clip)
Three GPIO that double as green/red/blue LEDs
Pico-compatible pinout

hdmi_capture.note: It is video OUT only. It cannot capture or ingest video from anything - a common misreading of the name.

uart.note: Talks to the Flipper over the Expansion Module Protocol on USART (pins 13/14) or LPUART (15/16); the breakout GPIO can drive your own serial links.

i2c.note: Available on the breakout GPIO if you program the RP2040 yourself; nothing in the stock firmware uses it.

spi_flash_dump.note: No such function exists in the shipped firmware. You could write one, but a bare Pico is a better base.

logic_analyzer.note: Not implemented. The PIO units could do it, but nobody has shipped it for this board.

scriptable.note: Fully user-programmable, but in C against the Raspberry Pi Pico SDK - not scripting. Flash by UF2 drag-and-drop, or from the Flipper itself with the Video Game Module Tool app.

usb_mass_storage.note: Enumerates as a UF2 mass-storage volume in bootloader mode for flashing. Not a general storage feature.

standalone_untethered.note: Runs standalone on USB-C power as an ordinary RP2040 board, but its Flipper-facing features obviously need the Flipper.

legal.notes: No restrictions found anywhere. This board has no radio and adds no transmit capability of any kind, so it raises none of the radio-law questions the Flipper itself does. It is, legally speaking, a Raspberry Pi Pico with a video connector.

ecosystem.app_store: Technically yes, but only about 5-6 of roughly 441 official catalog apps target it, and most of those are Flipper's own demos
